tasks.description: Identify the key client-side stakeholders and internal team members and record them in a single register the team actually uses. DONE only if: a register exists in the project space listing both client and internal people with role, decision authority, and contact channel; it covers the people the team really escalates to (cross-check against recent meetings and threads); and it names who signs off on scope and release decisions.
tasks.risk: Without a clear map of who on the client side decides what, the team wastes days chasing the right approver, receives conflicting instructions from different people, and important updates never reach the one person who could have acted on them. Each of these translates directly into stalled work and missed dates.

tasks.description: Agree and document one official channel for client correspondence so requests and decisions live in a single accountable place. DONE only if: the channel (e.g. Slack Connect, email) is named in project documentation together with what counts as an official request; the client contacts from the stakeholder register are present in it; and a spot-check shows recent scope and priority decisions recorded there rather than in personal DMs.
tasks.risk: When requests and decisions arrive through personal chats and scattered mailboxes, some get lost and work is done that was never properly agreed. And when a disagreement later arises about scope, priorities, or cost, there is no single record to settle it - misunderstandings turn into disputes about who pays for the extra work.

tasks.body: Set up BE communication channel & recurring BE sync (by PM or TL)
tasks.description: Give backend developers a dedicated channel and a recurring sync to align on API design, database changes, and technical blockers before they diverge. DONE only if: the channel exists with every BE developer in it and shows real technical discussion; a recurring BE sync is on the calendar with an agreed cadence; and decisions from it (API contracts, schema changes) are traceable in notes or channel history. Applies only to teams with more than one BE developer; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Without a regular place for the developers to align, two people can unknowingly build the same thing twice, or build pieces that turn out not to fit together. The mismatch is discovered late, when fixing it is at its most expensive, and the schedule absorbs the cost.

tasks.body: Compare WBS with team commitment (by PM)
tasks.description: Check the Work Breakdown Structure against what the team can actually deliver before anyone commits to dates. DONE only if: the WBS is decomposed to estimable items; a documented comparison of estimates against available team capacity exists; and any mismatch was resolved on record - scope cut, timeline moved, or team extended - rather than silently absorbed.
tasks.risk: If the plan is never checked against what the team can realistically deliver, the project starts with commitments that are impossible to keep. That gap surfaces later as missed deadlines and an exhausted team - at a point where renegotiating scope or dates is far harder and more expensive than it would have been on day one.

tasks.description: Start the service from a deliberately chosen, standard starter for the stack (NestJS, Django, Spring, etc.) rather than an ad-hoc skeleton, and choose the compute platform (EC2, Lambda, ECS, Kubernetes, etc.) in the same kickoff discussion - the boilerplate must fit the platform it will run on (cold starts, statefulness, scaling model). DONE only if: the chosen boilerplate and compute platform are recorded together with the reasons for both; the repository demonstrably descends from the boilerplate (structure and baseline configs match); the deployed runtime matches the recorded platform decision; and anything the starter lacked - lint, test, CI scaffolding - was consciously added rather than left out.
tasks.risk: A carelessly chosen technical foundation is like building on the wrong plot of land: months in, the system cannot handle growth or run cost-effectively, and parts of it have to be rebuilt. An hour of comparison at the start turns into weeks of unplanned rework and surprise hosting bills later.

tasks.description: Choose the database engine and file-storage approach through a documented, criteria-based comparison, not by habit or preference. DONE only if: a scoring or comparison record exists weighing candidates against project criteria (data shape, access patterns, consistency, scale, cost, team expertise); the engine and storage actually in use are the ones the analysis selected; and the decision is captured with its context where it can be revisited (ADR or kickoff doc). The living data model/ERD is assessed separately under Data & Persistence.
tasks.risk: If the place where all the project's data lives is chosen out of habit rather than analysis, it may prove unable to handle the real volume and kinds of data once the business grows. Moving everything to a different one mid-project is among the most expensive and risky operations a project can face, often freezing new feature work for weeks.

tasks.body: Define branching model (branching, commit naming, tagging rules)
tasks.description: Define the branching model together with branch naming, commit message, and tagging rules in one place. DONE only if: a single document states the model (GitFlow, trunk-based, etc.) plus branch, commit, and tag conventions; and the repository history actually follows it - spot-checked branch names, commit messages, and release tags match the documented rules. Machine enforcement of these rules is graded separately under the Conventions gate in Delivery Workflow.
tasks.risk: Without agreed rules for how developers combine their work, changes overwrite each other during release preparation, and nobody can say with certainty which version of the system customers are actually using. Every urgent fix then becomes a gamble that can make an incident worse instead of better.

tasks.description: Connect the repository to Jira so branches, commits, and PRs link to tickets automatically. DONE only if: the integration is installed and active; recent Jira issues show linked branches, commits, and PRs in the development panel - not just an installed plugin; and commit messages carry ticket keys so any code change traces back to its requirement.
tasks.risk: When code changes are not automatically linked to the tasks that requested them, the project board stops reflecting reality - managers report progress that does not match what was truly delivered. Later, working out which change caused a problem, or proving a requirement was actually built, becomes slow manual detective work.

tasks.description: Wire the repository and pipeline into the team messenger so PRs, failed builds, and deployments announce themselves. DONE only if: notifications post into an agreed channel; they cover at least PR events and pipeline failures/deployments; and recent messages in that channel prove the wiring is live, not configured-and-forgotten.
tasks.risk: If nobody is automatically told when finished work is waiting for a colleague's check, or when a delivery step has failed, completed work sits idle for days and breakages go unnoticed until someone stumbles on them. This quiet drag adds up to visibly slower delivery every single week.

tasks.description: Make uniform editor behavior a property of the repository, not of individual machines - personal IDE settings cannot be audited, committed artifacts can. DONE only if: shared editor and formatter configuration is committed (.editorconfig plus the formatter/linter configs the IDEs consume); a recommended plugin/extension list is committed or documented (e.g. .vscode/extensions.json covering linter and SonarLint-class tools); and recent diffs show no formatting or style drift between authors.
tasks.risk: When every developer's tools style the code slightly differently, colleagues checking each other's work spend their time on cosmetic differences instead of real mistakes. Reviews take longer, avoidable defects slip through, and every change costs a little more than it should.

tasks.description: Configure the package registries the project depends on and make accidental publication of internal code impossible. DONE only if: registry configuration (.npmrc, pip.conf, settings.xml, etc.) is committed or documented so any developer and CI can resolve every dependency, private ones included; registry credentials are injected at build time, never committed; and internal packages are explicitly marked private or scoped to the internal registry ('private': true, publishConfig, or the stack's equivalent).
tasks.risk: New team members and the automated delivery process can grind to a halt because they cannot access the building blocks the project depends on - days lost on setup instead of delivery. Worse, without the right safeguards a single careless command can publish the client's private code to the public internet, where it can never be fully taken back.

tasks.body: Local dev environment runs via docker-compose
tasks.description: A new developer must get a working local environment from a clean checkout with one command, and it must resemble production. DONE only if: the repository contains a compose file that starts the application together with every backing dependency it needs (database, cache, queue, etc.); the documented startup command works from a fresh clone without undocumented manual steps; dependency versions in the compose file match the production engines at least at major-version level.
tasks.risk: Every new developer loses days of paid time just getting set up before they can do useful work, and because each person's setup differs from the live system, the team regularly burns hours chasing problems that only exist on one machine - or misses ones that will surface in front of real users.

tasks.body: AI tooling configured (Cursor rules, spec, recon)
tasks.description: AI coding assistants must be steered by project-specific configuration committed to the repository, not used bare. DONE only if: the repo contains AI rules files (Cursor rules, CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, or equivalent) that encode the project's stack, conventions, and architecture; a spec/recon workflow for AI-assisted tasks is set up and referenced in the project docs; the rules describe the codebase as it currently is, not a stale or generic template.
tasks.risk: AI coding tools used without project-specific guidance produce work that looks correct but doesn't fit how this system is actually built, quietly adding bugs and inconsistency faster than people can catch them. A tool bought to speed up delivery ends up slowing it down and raising the cost of every future change.

tasks.description: Every change reaches the main branches only through a reviewed pull request, and the review rules are explicit rather than tribal. DONE only if: branch protection requires the agreed number of approving reviews plus green CI before merge, with direct pushes to protected branches blocked; review expectations and checklist are documented; recent merged PRs show real review activity - comments and change requests exist, and PRs are not routinely self-approved or merged unreviewed.
tasks.risk: Changes can reach the live system without a second person ever looking at them, so mistakes a colleague would have caught in minutes go straight to users - and product quality depends entirely on each developer's discipline on any given day.

tasks.body: Conventions gate: linting, formatting, commit rules enforced
tasks.description: Coding standards count only when a machine enforces them. DONE only if: linter and formatter configurations are committed to the repository; they run automatically via pre-commit hooks and/or a blocking CI step that fails on violations (warn-only does not count); commit messages are validated against the agreed convention (commitlint or equivalent); the current codebase actually passes the gate.
tasks.risk: Standards that no machine enforces fade within weeks: the codebase becomes inconsistent and harder to read, every future change takes longer and costs more, and the change history stops explaining what was done and why - exactly the information needed when something breaks and the cause must be found fast.

tasks.description: Build, test, and deployment are automated end-to-end. DONE only if: the pipeline definition lives in the repository; every push or PR triggers build and tests, and merges deploy automatically to at least a staging environment; recent run history is green - a pipeline that has been red or skipped for weeks scores as absent.
tasks.risk: Releasing new versions depends on someone performing manual steps by hand, so an urgent fix takes hours instead of minutes to reach users, and every release carries a real chance of a human mistake taking the system down.

tasks.description: The path from merged code to production must be written down, not carried in one person's head. DONE only if: a release document lists every environment with its details, the step-by-step release procedure, and the responsible person or role for each step; the document matches how the pipeline currently works - stale instructions score as absent. Rollback is assessed by its own task, not here.
tasks.risk: If the release steps live only in one person's head, the company cannot ship updates - including urgent fixes - while that person is on vacation, sick, or gone, and anyone forced to improvise in their place risks breaking the live system.

tasks.description: When a release goes bad, the team must be able to return to the previous stable version quickly - and the mechanism must be proven, not theoretical. DONE only if: the rollback procedure for both the application and database migrations is documented and scripted or automated; previous release artifacts are retained and redeployable; there is evidence the rollback has been exercised at least once (a drill or a real incident); irreversible migrations have a stated forward-fix plan.
tasks.risk: If an update goes wrong, there is no proven way to return to the last working version: the team has to improvise live and under pressure, and an ordinary bad release turns into hours or days of the system being unavailable to every user.

tasks.description: Production deployments must deliberately limit downtime and blast radius - blue/green, canary, or health-gated rolling deployments are all acceptable. DONE only if: the chosen strategy is named and documented; the deployment configuration demonstrably implements it (health-gated rolling-update settings, weighted traffic shifting, or a duplicate-environment switch); a failed health check halts or reverts the rollout instead of replacing all instances with a broken build.
tasks.risk: Every update reaches all users at once, so a faulty release hits the entire customer base instantly instead of a small test group - and even a routine, healthy release can mean a visible outage window each time.

tasks.description: Application configuration comes from environment variables or a config service, with a separate and complete set per environment. DONE only if: no environment-specific values (URLs, hostnames, feature flags) are hardcoded in the codebase; every environment - dev and test/stage included, not only prod - has its own full config set with no silent fallback to another environment's values; required variables are documented and kept current (e.g. .env.example). Secret storage itself is assessed under Security & Compliance.
tasks.risk: A mix-up between test and live settings can make a test run touch the real system - sending real emails, moving real money, or overwriting real customer data - and this kind of incident is typically discovered only after the damage is done.

tasks.description: Knowledge of each module must not concentrate in a single head, and review duty must circulate. DONE only if: ownership is explicit (CODEOWNERS or a documented owner map covering the main modules); recent PR history shows multiple distinct reviewers rather than one person approving everything; every critical module has at least two people who have recently written or reviewed code in it. Applies only to teams with more than one BE developer; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: If only one person understands a critical part of the system, all work on it stops the day that person is on leave or resigns, leaving delivery hostage to a single employee's availability - and a lone permanent reviewer eventually waves changes through without really checking them.

tasks.description: Design patterns are applied where they genuinely solve a recurring problem, in a form idiomatic to the stack - and not forced where a plain function would do. DONE only if: recurring variation points (multiple providers, notification channels, object construction) are handled through recognizable patterns (strategy, factory, adapter, etc.) rather than growing if/else or switch chains; every pattern found in the code is justified by an actual need, with no pattern-for-pattern's-sake scaffolding such as a factory over a single implementation; pattern implementations use the framework's idioms rather than hand-rolled reinventions.
tasks.risk: Every time the business wants to add a new option - a new payment provider, a new way to notify users - developers must hand-edit many scattered places instead of plugging the addition into one, so simple additions take weeks instead of days and each one risks breaking something that already worked.

tasks.description: No god classes: each class or service does one job and stays within a measurable size bound. DONE only if: no class exceeds the agreed threshold (default: ~400 lines per class and the Sonar cognitive-complexity limit per function) without a written, reviewed justification; the largest classes in the codebase were actually opened and each still has a single reason to change; static-analysis output (Sonar or equivalent) shows no critical size/complexity violations.
tasks.risk: When too much of the application is crammed into one oversized piece, every developer ends up working in the same spot at once: they block each other, delivery slows, and a change made for one feature can unexpectedly break a completely unrelated one.

tasks.description: Each piece of logic, each service, and each model exists exactly once. DONE only if: Sonar duplication density is within the agreed threshold (default <=3%); there is no family of copy-pasted services or modules differing only in a few lines (spot-check similarly named files across features); there are no parallel DTO/model sets describing the same data shape twice.
tasks.risk: When the same logic exists in several copied places, a bug fixed in one copy quietly lives on in the others - so customers keep hitting a problem the team already reported as fixed, and every fix costs several times what it should.

tasks.description: Dependencies flow in one direction - outer layers depend on inner ones, never the reverse - and modules stay loosely coupled. DONE only if: domain/application code contains no imports of web, persistence, or infrastructure implementations; services are wired through the DI container, not manual construction or service locators; a module-dependency check (madge, ArchUnit, deptrac, or a manual import review) shows no cycles between modules; no code reaches across a feature boundary into another feature's internals such as its repositories or private services.
tasks.risk: When every part of the system is entangled with every other, fixing one thing routinely breaks something elsewhere. The team ends up spending more time repairing side effects than delivering new work, and eventually becomes afraid to change anything at all.

tasks.description: Everything the application opens, it also closes. DONE only if: every executor/thread pool, connection, stream, and subscription created by application code has a matching shutdown or close wired into the framework's lifecycle hooks; the service handles SIGTERM gracefully - stops accepting new work, finishes or hands off in-flight tasks, and closes pools before exit; a code search for executor/client/stream construction finds none created ad hoc without disposal.
tasks.risk: The application slowly consumes more and more of its own resources until it crashes at seemingly random moments - outages nobody can quickly explain - and every software update can cut off tasks that were still in progress, losing that work.

tasks.description: Complexity must be bought by a real need, not by 'we might need it later'. DONE only if: abstractions (interfaces, generic layers, plugin mechanisms) have at least two real implementations or a concrete, documented upcoming need; reading the code surfaces no dead configurability, unused extension points, or speculative generality; straightforward problems are solved with the stack's idiomatic, straightforward tools.
tasks.risk: Machinery built 'just in case' never pays off but must be maintained forever: every small change costs more than it should, new team members take far longer to become productive, and budget goes into upkeep instead of the features the business actually asked for.

tasks.description: The codebase follows the house standard: feature-sliced organization with layered/onion boundaries inside each slice and domain-driven naming - and it is graded on what the code actually does, because folder names alone are not evidence. DONE only if: files spot-checked in each layer match that layer's role (controllers hold no business logic, domain code holds no persistence or transport concerns); features live in vertical slices so all code for a feature is co-located rather than spread across technical-only folders; domain types and services are named in the business's language, consistent with the project glossary.
tasks.risk: The project can look well organized on the surface while its core business rules are actually tangled into technical plumbing - so changing a rule like pricing, permissions, or order flow becomes slow and risky, and mistakes in those rules are hard to catch before customers see them.

tasks.description: Dependencies are maintained, justified, and kept current. DONE only if: every significant dependency is actively maintained (no archived or deprecated projects on critical paths), or its choice is explicitly argued in an ADR/docs; no heavy library is imported for something the standard library or framework already provides; update activity is visible in history - merged Renovate/Dependabot PRs or recurring update tasks - and no critical dependency sits more than one major version behind without a documented plan.
tasks.risk: When the outside software the system is built on is abandoned or left badly out of date, its known problems and security holes will never be fixed - and catching up later turns into a large, expensive, risky project of its own instead of routine maintenance.

tasks.description: The runtime and language versions are supported, and upgrades are planned rather than deferred until forced. DONE only if: the project runs on a currently supported (non-EOL) runtime/language version; the framework's major version is inside its official support window; for any version approaching EOL, a migration task exists in the backlog scheduled before the EOL date.
tasks.risk: Once the foundation the application runs on passes its end-of-support date, security fixes for it simply stop arriving, leaving known holes open. The only way out is then a rushed, high-risk upgrade at the worst possible moment - often forced by an urgent security problem.

tasks.description: No outbound dependency may hang the service or be retried into a storm. DONE only if: every outbound client - HTTP, database, cache, queue - has explicit connect and read/request timeouts configured, with library defaults of infinite/unbounded counting as a fail; retries are bounded with backoff and applied only to idempotent operations; failure of a dependency surfaces as a fast, handled error rather than blocked threads, with a circuit breaker or equivalent where the dependency is on a critical path.
tasks.risk: A slowdown at a single external service - a payment provider, an email sender - can freeze the entire application and take it offline for all users, so the system goes down because of someone else's problem; badly configured automatic retries can then make the outage even longer.

tasks.description: Any operation with an external effect must survive being delivered twice, because retries and redeliveries are routine. DONE only if: endpoints and consumers that create payments, orders, or other external effects deduplicate replays via idempotency keys, processed-event-id storage, or natural-key upserts; webhook handlers tolerate redelivery of the same event without repeating the effect; retried jobs and at-least-once queue consumers are shown - in code or tests - not to double-apply.
tasks.risk: An ordinary network hiccup can cause the same payment or order to be processed twice - customers are charged double or receive duplicate orders, and the business learns about it through refund demands and disputes rather than from the system itself.

tasks.description: The database selection decision is closed at kickoff; this is the living half: a documented data model (ERD or collection/schema map) that still matches what is actually deployed. DONE only if: the model exists at a known location and covers all core entities/collections; a spot-check of 3-5 core entities against the actual schema or ORM models shows matching fields and relations in both directions; schema changes made since the previous assessment (visible in recent migrations) are reflected in the model.
tasks.risk: New features get built against an outdated picture of how the system's information is organized, which leads to mistakes that duplicate or corrupt data - and every new developer must first spend days rediscovering how things really work before they can safely change anything, slowing all future delivery.

tasks.description: Indexes exist for the queries the application actually runs, not just primary keys. DONE only if: filter, sort, and join columns on the hottest query paths - identified from real endpoint code - are backed by indexes visible in the schema or migrations; query plans (EXPLAIN / explain()) or slow-query logs/APM for those paths show index usage, not full scans; foreign keys used in joins are indexed, and no redundant duplicate indexes are accumulating write cost.
tasks.risk: The application gets slower as real data accumulates: searches and lists that felt instant during demos start taking many seconds or failing outright, and this slowdown typically surfaces as an outage exactly when the business starts to grow.

tasks.body: Transactions used where atomicity is required
tasks.description: Multi-step writes that must succeed or fail together actually run atomically. DONE only if: the state-critical multi-write flows (payments, orders, balance updates, multi-document changes) are identified and each runs inside an explicit transaction or an equivalent atomic construct (single-document update, upsert); no reviewed flow can leave inconsistent state when a failure lands between dependent writes; failures trigger rollback - no code path commits partial work or swallows the error and continues. Applies only to databases with transactional semantics (relational, Mongo multi-doc, etc.); applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: If the system fails midway through a multi-step operation, it can leave things half-done - for example, a customer's money is taken but no order is ever created. Every such case means manual clean-up, a refund, and a dispute with an unhappy customer.

tasks.description: Transactions wrap only the statements that need atomicity, and stay short. DONE only if: no external calls (HTTP, message publishing, email, file storage) execute inside a transaction boundary in the reviewed flows; no transaction spans long computation or an unbounded loop, and batch jobs commit in chunks rather than in one giant transaction; hot-path transactions touch a bounded, known set of rows/documents. Applies only to databases with transactional semantics; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: One slow response from an outside service can freeze many unrelated operations at once, so during busy periods the whole application can grind to a halt and look like it is down - even though nothing is actually broken, and finding the real cause takes hours.

tasks.description: Concurrent writers to the same data are handled deliberately, not by luck. DONE only if: flows that update the same rows/documents concurrently use a consistent approach - stable lock ordering, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or optimistic versioning with conflict handling; deadlock and serialization errors are caught and retried with bounded backoff instead of reaching users or being silently ignored; deadlocks and lock waits are observable in engine logs or monitoring, and current figures were checked during the assessment. Applies only to databases with transactional semantics; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: When many customers use the system at the same time, some of their actions - including payments or orders - can randomly fail in ways that never appear during testing; these failures are extremely hard to trace and steadily erode users' trust in the product.

tasks.body: Schema normalized to fit access patterns
tasks.description: OLTP tables keep each fact in exactly one place, in a normal form that fits how the application reads and writes. DONE only if: a spot-check of core tables shows no repeated-value columns (addr1/addr2/addr3), no delimiter-packed ID lists, and no copies of mutable data without a documented reason; relations are modeled with foreign keys and join tables rather than duplicated columns; update flows change a given fact in one place only. Applies only to relational databases; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: The same piece of information ends up stored in several places, so an update in one place leaves outdated values elsewhere - customers see contradictory details, and staff spend ongoing time manually correcting records instead of trusting the system.

tasks.description: Where the schema does duplicate data - read models, counters, cached aggregates - it is a recorded decision with a sync mechanism, not accidental drift. DONE only if: every denormalized structure found in the schema maps to a written justification (ADR or data-model doc) naming the access pattern it serves; each has a defined mechanism keeping the copy consistent (trigger, event handler, scheduled rebuild) with its failure mode handled; no duplicated columns remain that the team cannot explain. Applies only to relational databases; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Duplicate copies of data quietly drift apart until reports and screens show different numbers for the same thing; at that point nobody can say which figure is correct, and business decisions may be made on wrong numbers while the team spends days untangling which value to trust.

tasks.description: Every schema, index, and reference-data change is versioned and applied by a migration tool - for any engine: a document-store tool (Mongock, migrate-mongo) satisfies this exactly as Liquibase or Flyway does for SQL, and must never score lower for not being relational. DONE only if: a migration tool for the project's actual engine is present and runs as part of deployment or a documented release step; recent schema/index changes each trace to a migration file, none applied manually through a console - verified by comparing migration history against the live schema; the tool tracks applied migrations (ordering, checksums) so every environment converges on the identical set.
tasks.risk: Changes to how data is stored get made by hand and end up differing between the test system and the live one, so a release that worked perfectly in testing can crash the live system - and recovery takes far longer because nobody knows exactly what state that system is in.

tasks.body: No N+1 queries; list endpoints paginated
tasks.description: Data access must scale with page size, not with table size. DONE only if: hot list endpoints load relations via joins, eager loading, or batching - the dev/CI query log shows a constant number of queries per request rather than one per returned row; every collection endpoint enforces a server-side default and maximum page size, so a request without pagination parameters cannot return an entire table; an N+1 guard is active (ORM lazy-load warnings, query-count assertions in tests, or APM rules), or at minimum the auditor's query-log check of the top endpoints found none.
tasks.risk: Screens that respond instantly with a handful of demo records become dramatically heavier as real data accumulates - a single busy page can overload the system and make the application unavailable for everyone, often triggered by the first sizable customer.

tasks.body: No secrets in repository or git history
tasks.description: The repository must contain no live credentials - not in the working tree and not anywhere in git history, since a secret committed once is recoverable forever. DONE only if: a secret scanner (gitleaks, trufflehog, or platform-native secret scanning) has been run over the full git history and reports no live findings; every credential ever found in history has been rotated, not merely deleted in a later commit; scanning runs continuously (pre-commit hook, CI job, or repo-host secret scanning) so new leaks are caught at push time.
tasks.risk: Passwords and access keys that were ever saved into the project's code remain extractable from its history forever - anyone who ever receives a copy, including former contractors, can use them to reach the live system, and such leaks are usually discovered only after someone has already abused them.

tasks.description: Authentication and authorization must be enforced globally, so an endpoint is protected unless explicitly declared public - never the reverse. DONE only if: the framework's global auth mechanism (global guard, security filter chain, middleware) is enabled application-wide, not disabled and re-added per controller or per endpoint; anonymous endpoints form an explicit allow-list (public decorator, permitAll entries) the auditor can enumerate and justify; authorization (role/ownership checks) is present on protected resources and verified by attempting to fetch another user's resource and receiving 403/404.
tasks.risk: Every new feature goes live open to the internet unless a developer remembers to switch protection on - a single forgotten step silently exposes customer data, and nothing in the process is positioned to catch the mistake before an outsider finds it.

tasks.description: Every credential the system accepts - user tokens and calls from external systems (webhooks, partner APIs) - must be cryptographically verified, and any verification failure or error must reject the request rather than let it through. DONE only if: JWT handling validates signature, expiry, issuer, and audience (not just decodes the payload); every inbound webhook endpoint verifies the provider's signature or shared secret before processing the payload; the failure path is fail-closed - a tampered, unsigned, or verification-erroring request is rejected, confirmed by sending one in a test environment.
tasks.risk: An outsider who discovers the right address can send the system fake messages that look like they come from a trusted partner - for example a fabricated "payment received" notice - and the system will act on them, releasing goods or services without any money actually arriving.

tasks.description: User input must never be able to change the shape of a query or command - only its parameters. DONE only if: a repo-wide review shows all database access goes through the ORM, query builders, or parameterized statements, with no string concatenation or interpolation of user input into SQL/NoSQL queries, shell commands, or eval-like constructs; user input reaching regexes or query operators (e.g. Mongo operators) is escaped or type-constrained; SAST injection rules are enabled and report no open findings.
tasks.risk: One weak spot of this kind is enough for an attacker to read out or erase the entire customer database - historically one of the most common causes of major breaches, with data-loss, legal, and reputational consequences far beyond the single feature that had the flaw.

tasks.description: Operational and debug interfaces must be unreachable to outsiders in production. DONE only if: management surfaces are inventoried (JMX, Spring Actuator, framework debug pages, GraphQL/ORM consoles, admin panels, profilers, Swagger UI, GraphQL introspection) and each is disabled in prod, bound to localhost/an internal network only, or protected by authentication; GraphQL introspection and interactive API docs specifically are confirmed off or auth-protected on production; this is verified against the actual production configuration - exposure found here is an automatic fail of this task.
tasks.risk: Internal control panels left reachable from the internet are found by automated scanners within hours, and can hand an outsider anything from stored passwords to full control of the system.

tasks.body: OWASP Top-10 review of remaining categories
tasks.description: The sibling checks in this area cover the highest-frequency OWASP categories (secrets, auth enforcement, token verification, injection, exposed management surfaces); this task explicitly closes the rest so no category is skipped for lack of a dedicated checkbox. DONE only if: the auditor records a per-category verdict with code/config evidence for each of the following: transport security - TLS enforced on every endpoint, no plaintext listeners; password storage and authentication flows - proper hashing, no home-grown crypto, brute-force protection on login; rate limiting and resource consumption - login/OTP/password-reset and expensive endpoints throttled, request body and upload size caps configured (graded here, not as a separate task); object-level access control - a user cannot read or modify another user's resources by substituting an id; security misconfiguration - no default credentials, no verbose errors or stack traces in prod responses, security headers present; software and data integrity - no insecure deserialization of untrusted input, dependencies and build artifacts from trusted sources only; SSRF - any endpoint that fetches user-supplied URLs validates and restricts targets.
tasks.risk: The less common attack routes that never got their own checklist item simply go unexamined year after year - and companies are regularly breached through exactly the door nobody thought to check.

tasks.description: From the code's perspective, secrets must live outside the codebase: configuration files carry references, and real values arrive from the environment at runtime. DONE only if: committed config files (application.yml, appsettings, config modules) contain no plaintext credentials for any environment; secrets are loaded via environment variables or a secret-store client through the config layer; .env and similar local-secret files are git-ignored with only a placeholder .env.example committed; per-environment configs are separated so production values never appear in dev/test files.
tasks.risk: Passwords written directly into project files travel with every copy of the code, giving anyone who sees them direct access to servers and client data. Mixed-up environment settings can also cause test activity to hit the real live system, affecting real customers.

tasks.description: On the platform side, production secrets must live in a dedicated secrets manager rather than scattered across CI variables, deploy scripts, and chats. DONE only if: production secrets are stored in a managed store (AWS SSM/Secrets Manager, Vault, or equivalent) and injected at deploy or runtime; access is scoped least-privilege - the application role reads only its own secrets and developers hold no blanket production read access; a rotation procedure exists and works without code changes, evidenced by a documented past rotation or a tested runbook.
tasks.risk: When passwords and keys are scattered across tools, chats, and notes instead of kept in one managed place, containing a leak takes days instead of minutes - nobody can quickly find and replace every copy, so an attacker keeps working keys to the live system the whole time.

tasks.description: Production CORS must allow-list concrete trusted origins, and the check must be performed at whichever layer actually terminates CORS - application middleware, API gateway, or nginx - using that layer's real production config. DONE only if: no wildcard origin in prod and no reflection of arbitrary Origin headers, especially never combined with credentials; allowed methods and headers are restricted to what clients actually use; the auditor has inspected the terminating layer's production configuration, not the app defaults that a proxy in front may override.
tasks.risk: Any website a user happens to visit could quietly read that user's data through their own logged-in session - and because every request looks like normal user activity, the theft leaves no trace anyone would notice.

tasks.description: When a vulnerability drops in a dependency, the team must react by process, not by luck. DONE only if: a documented workflow names who receives vulnerability alerts and defines a patch SLA by severity (e.g. criticals within days); alerting is actually wired - Dependabot/Snyk/Renovate notifications land in a channel someone monitors; the process demonstrably ran at least once - a past advisory traceable to its upgrade ticket and release.
tasks.risk: When a serious flaw is publicly announced in one of the ready-made components the system is built on, attackers start exploiting it within hours; without an assigned owner and a standing routine, the team learns about the hole from the client - or from the break-in itself.

tasks.description: Vulnerability discovery in dependencies and images must be automatic and recurring, not something a human remembers to run. DONE only if: dependency scanning (Snyk, Dependabot, npm audit in CI, OWASP Dependency-Check) runs on every build or a fixed schedule; where the project ships containers, images are scanned (Trivy, registry-native scanning) before deployment; findings surface where the team actually looks, with critical severities blocking or alerting rather than accumulating in an unread report.
tasks.risk: Without automatic checking, the system keeps shipping components with publicly known security holes for months, and nobody even knows the risk is on board until someone exploits it.

tasks.description: Static security analysis must run inside the delivery pipeline so every change is checked before it ships. DONE only if: SAST (Sonar security rules, Semgrep, CodeQL, or equivalent) executes on every pipeline run; findings gate the pipeline at an agreed severity - new critical findings fail the build or force explicit triage; the gate is demonstrably live, not a scanner that has been red or muted for months while merges continue.
tasks.risk: Each new release can introduce a fresh security hole with no one checking before it goes live - the problem then surfaces only after the system has already been broken into, when fixing it is at its most expensive and most public.

tasks.description: Verify concretely that backend engineers hold no more access than their current work requires, across every system the project touches. DONE only if: the audit enumerates the BE engineers' actual grants in the repo host (membership via teams/groups, not one-off individual invites), cloud accounts, databases, and third-party services, and each grant maps to a present need; no admin/owner roles where write or read suffices, and no standing production database write access or personal long-lived keys where roles/SSO exist; recently offboarded members are confirmed absent from all of the above.
tasks.risk: Access handed out person-by-person and never reviewed means people who left the team can still reach live systems months later, and a single stolen developer account can turn into control of the company's entire cloud environment.

tasks.description: Every external service the backend depends on must be inventoried, owned correctly, and confirmed fit for the project's scale and lifetime. DONE only if: an inventory of third-party services (payments, email, storage, analytics, etc.) exists naming the account owner, the plan/tier, and test-vs-live key separation per environment; each account belongs to the client's or company's organization, not an engineer's personal email; each service is assessed as fit - pricing sustainable at projected volume, adequate SLA, not deprecated or being sunset - with any red flag recorded in the risk register.
tasks.risk: The business may quietly depend on an outside service that is about to become too expensive or shut down, forcing a rushed and costly migration - or discover that a critical account, such as payments or email, is registered to the personal address of someone who already left and could be lost at any moment.

tasks.description: Every shipped dependency's license must be verified compatible with commercial, closed-source use. DONE only if: an automated license scan (license-checker, Snyk, or equivalent) runs in CI or at each release; no copyleft-incompatible dependencies (GPL/AGPL family) are present in shipped code without explicit documented sign-off; a current license inventory is stored with the project docs and refreshed each release.
tasks.risk: A single ready-made component with the wrong license terms can trigger a lawsuit or legally force the company to give away its own product's source code for free - a business-level consequence of one unchecked download.

tasks.body: No PII or secrets in logs & telemetry
tasks.description: Logs, error trackers, and traces must never carry credentials or personal data in plaintext - telemetry is the least-protected copy of production data. DONE only if: logging and error-tracker configuration shows active redaction (logger serializers/denylists, Sentry beforeSend or server-side scrubbing) for tokens, passwords, auth headers, and personal/card data; full request/response body logging is disabled or masked on sensitive routes; a spot-check of real staging or production log output confirms nothing sensitive appears.
tasks.risk: The system's internal activity records become an extra, poorly guarded copy of customer data: if they leak or too many people can view them, that alone is a reportable data breach with potential fines, and sign-in details captured there let anyone with viewing access act as real users.

tasks.description: The project's code is continuously analyzed on the Geniusee self-hosted SonarQube so that quality, duplication, complexity, and coverage exist as objective numbers - this is the evidence base several other checks in this area and in Architecture rely on. DONE only if: the project exists on the Geniusee self-hosted SonarQube instance and analysis runs automatically on merges to the main development branch (not a one-off manual scan); the analyzed branch is the branch the team actually develops on; coverage and duplication metrics are populated (a 0%/empty coverage panel from a misconfigured scanner does not pass).
tasks.risk: Without an independent, automatic measurement of the code's health, the only source of truth is the team grading its own work - quality can quietly decline for months, and by the time it surfaces as bugs and slower delivery, there are no objective numbers to show when it started or how bad it is.

tasks.body: Unit/integration testing framework with fixed coverage expectation
tasks.description: A unit/integration testing framework is set up and runnable, and the company coverage expectation applies to this project as a given: 80% unless a different figure was explicitly agreed at kickoff - this is expected from everyone, it is not a per-project negotiation. DONE only if: the framework (Jest, PyTest, JUnit, etc.) is configured in the repository with a single documented command that runs the suite locally and in CI; coverage reporting is configured and produces an actual figure; the expected threshold is written down in repo config or project docs, not agreed verbally.
tasks.risk: If automated testing is not set up with a clear, agreed bar, verifying that things still work falls back to people manually clicking through the application - slow, incomplete, and the first thing skipped under deadline pressure - so features that used to work quietly break and reach real users.

tasks.description: The coverage expectation must be machine-enforced somewhere, not aspirational: a change that drops coverage below the agreed figure must fail an automated check. DONE only if: a blocking gate exists - a CI step that fails the build, a Sonar quality gate that fails the analysis, or equivalent - configured with the agreed threshold; the auditor can point to a pipeline run or PR where the gate actually executed; the gate cannot be routinely bypassed (not marked optional/informational, no continue-on-error, no habit of merging on red).
tasks.risk: A testing standard that nothing enforces erodes one small change at a time: months later most of the system runs without a safety net even though no one ever decided to accept that, and breakages start reaching customers before anyone realizes the protection is gone.

tasks.description: Unit tests written and maintained by the backend team verify business logic in isolation, and sufficiency is judged by the measured coverage figure against the agreed expectation - 'some tests exist' is not a pass. DONE only if: a current coverage figure is produced by the configured reporting and meets the expectation; the tests exercise real business logic rather than padding the number with trivial getters, DTOs, and generated code; the tests live in the BE repository and run in the BE pipeline - suites owned by a separate QA/AQA team do not count toward this item.
tasks.risk: If only a small fraction of the business logic is genuinely tested, mistakes in the untested majority go straight into the client's operations - as wrong prices, wrong balances, or incorrect records - and are typically discovered by the client's own customers rather than by the team.

tasks.description: Critical flows are verified end-to-end through real wiring (API to services to database and integrations) by tests the backend team owns and runs - a separate AQA team's suite lives outside the BE repo, does not run on BE merges, and does not protect BE refactoring, so it does not satisfy this item. DONE only if: integration/E2E tests exist in the BE-owned repository and cover the critical flows (authentication, money movement, the main domain scenarios); they run in the BE pipeline per merge or on a schedule and the latest run is green; each covered critical flow is traceable to a named test in the BE repository whose failure blocks the BE merge.
tasks.risk: If the team relies on a separate group's test suite, a change that breaks sign-in or payments is not caught at the moment it is made - it is discovered days later by another team, or by customers who suddenly cannot log in or pay.

tasks.description: Load/performance tests exist for the highest-traffic and heaviest endpoints and flows, and their results are compared against explicit targets (drawn from the NFRs where those are defined). DONE only if: performance test scripts (k6, Gatling, Locust, JMeter, etc.) are version-controlled; there are recorded results from a run against a production-like environment; results are evaluated against stated latency/throughput targets, and any regression or capacity gap has a tracked follow-up ticket.
tasks.risk: Without testing how the system behaves under heavy use, the first real stress test is live traffic - a marketing campaign or busy season - and capacity problems arrive as a public outage at exactly the moment the business is most visible, instead of as a ticket fixed in advance.

tasks.description: Automated tests owned by the backend team verify the API surface - status codes, response payload shapes, the unified error structure, and authorization behavior - so a contract-breaking change fails the build instead of the clients. DONE only if: API-level tests exist in the BE repository and run in BE CI; they assert status codes and response structure for the main endpoints including error and unauthorized cases, not only 200 happy paths; the latest run is green; as with the sibling items, suites owned by a separate QA team do not count.
tasks.risk: A small change on the server can quietly break the website and mobile apps that depend on it: to users the product simply stops working, and because the server itself appears healthy, the failure is found by customers instead of being caught before release.

tasks.description: Two different things hide under this item and must not be conflated: consumer-driven contract testing (Pact and similar), which mechanically prevents breaking an independent consumer, and shared API collections (Postman/Insomnia/Bruno), which aid manual verification and handover. DONE only if: the project has declared which of the two it needs - contract testing where services or clients deploy on independent cycles, collections as a documented working aid, or neither with the rationale recorded at kickoff; whatever is declared actually exists and is current (Pact contracts verified in CI, or collections versioned and matching the present API); a Postman collection is never accepted as evidence of contract testing.
tasks.risk: The team mistakes a manual reference document for real automated protection, so a change that breaks a connected application or partner system passes unnoticed - the failure surfaces live, on someone else's side, where it is slowest and most expensive to trace back.

tasks.description: The application logger is set up for machine-parseable, leveled, correlated output - not ad-hoc console prints. DONE only if: logs are emitted in a structured format (JSON or equivalent key-value) that the log platform can parse and filter; log levels are used consistently and are configurable per environment; a correlation/request ID is generated or propagated for every request or consumed message and appears on every log line in its scope; bare console.log/print calls are not the de-facto logging mechanism (spot-check the codebase).
tasks.risk: When something breaks, the team has no quick way to pull up the records for the one affected customer or transaction - every incident turns into hours of manual searching while the system stays down and users wait.

tasks.body: Logs present in the right places with agreed structure
tasks.description: A configured logger is worthless if the flows where investigations start never call it - this task checks that logging actually exists where it matters. DONE only if: authentication, money-moving/business-critical flows, third-party integration calls, and error paths each emit entries with the agreed fields (actor, correlation ID, operation, outcome); reading the code of at least three critical flows confirms log statements at start, success, and failure - not just an eventual stack trace; the fields match the agreed structure so entries from different services are cross-searchable.
tasks.risk: If a payment or an exchange with an external service goes wrong, there is no record of what actually happened - the team cannot prove whether money moved once, twice, or not at all, and problems like this keep repeating because their cause is never found.

tasks.description: The service exports the basic request-level signals so degradation is visible before users report it. DONE only if: request rate, latency (percentiles, not only averages), and error rate are exported per endpoint/route to a metrics backend (Prometheus, CloudWatch, Datadog, etc.); the auditor can open a dashboard or run a query and see live data from the audited service; error rate is broken down at least by status class so a spike is attributable to specific endpoints.
tasks.risk: Nobody can see the system getting slower or failing more often until customers complain - and when they do, there is no history showing when the problem started or which change caused it, so investigations drag on while trust erodes.

tasks.description: The service reports its own health so the platform can restart or de-route broken instances without a human in the loop. DONE only if: liveness and readiness endpoints exist and differ meaningfully - readiness checks critical dependencies (e.g. database connectivity) while liveness stays cheap; the orchestrator or load balancer is actually configured to consume them (probe/target-group config verified in deployment manifests, not assumed); a health endpoint that exists but is wired to nothing does not pass.
tasks.risk: When one part of the system breaks, it keeps receiving customer traffic instead of being automatically restarted or taken out of rotation - outages that could resolve themselves in seconds instead last until someone notices and intervenes by hand, often after customers already have.

tasks.description: Logs from every service land in one searchable place - and that place is enough to reconstruct what happened to a specific user when they report a problem, across frontend errors, backend errors, logs, and traces. The tool choice (ELK, Loki, Datadog, Sentry plus correlated logs, OpenTelemetry) is irrelevant; the capability is what is graded. DONE only if: all deployed services ship logs to a single aggregation system, and one search returns matching entries from every service without shelling into any host; error tracking covers both backend and frontend and is joinable with logs and traces via shared identifiers (user ID, request/correlation ID); the auditor can take one recent real incident or user complaint and walk its full path end-to-end from the aggregated data alone; the retention period is defined and covers a realistic incident-investigation window.
tasks.risk: Answering 'what happened to this customer?' means digging through many separate systems by hand, and some records are permanently lost as servers are replaced - investigations that should take an hour take days, and some problems can never be explained at all.

tasks.description: Runtime internals - memory, garbage collection, event-loop lag or thread-pool saturation, average request time - are tracked to catch leaks and creeping degradation before they take the service down. DONE only if: runtime metrics appropriate to the platform (heap/memory usage, GC frequency and pause time, event-loop lag for Node, thread pools for JVM) are exported to the metrics backend; dashboards show their history over weeks so slow trends are visible, not just current values; abnormal memory growth is alertable or demonstrably reviewed.
tasks.risk: The system can degrade slowly and invisibly until it crashes - usually at the busiest moment, with no warning. Instead of fixing the cause, the team ends up restarting the system on a schedule, which is an ongoing cost and a standing risk of downtime.

tasks.description: The database's health is watched, not assumed. DONE only if: CPU, memory, connection count, and storage for the database are visible in a monitoring tool or cloud console the team actually uses; slow-query logging or a performance-insights feature is enabled and its output is reviewed; alerts exist for connection-pool exhaustion and storage thresholds rather than being discovered at outage time.
tasks.risk: The system's data storage can hit its limits without warning, taking the entire application down at once; and as the business grows, everything gets gradually slower with nobody able to say why - until it fails on the busiest day.

tasks.description: One application-wide handler owns every unhandled error so a single failure neither crashes the process nor leaks internals. DONE only if: a global middleware/exception filter is registered app-wide and covers all routes plus async paths (unhandled rejections, uncaught exceptions, background jobs); triggering an error against a deployed environment returns no raw stack trace or internal details to the client; every caught error is logged with context (correlation ID, route, user where available) and unexpected errors map to the unified error response rather than a blank 500.
tasks.risk: A single error in one feature can bring the whole system down for every user, or expose internal technical details that make an attacker's job easier - while other failures vanish without any trace, so the same bugs keep hurting users for months.

tasks.description: Every error the API returns follows one agreed structure - a semantically correct HTTP status plus a machine-readable error code (BAD_REQUEST, VALIDATION_FAILED, etc.) plus a consistent body shape - so clients handle failures programmatically instead of parsing message strings. DONE only if: the error schema is documented (status, code, human-readable message, optional field-level details); all error paths - validation, auth, not-found, unhandled 500s - return that same shape, verified by hitting real endpoints; HTTP statuses are used correctly (no 200-with-error-body, no blanket 500 for client mistakes).
tasks.risk: Users see a generic 'Something went wrong' instead of a message that tells them how to fix the problem, so support requests pile up for issues the application could have explained itself. Every app connected to the system also needs its own fragile workarounds, making future changes slower and more likely to break.

tasks.body: Compliance with API semantics (verbs, status codes, pagination)
tasks.description: Endpoints follow correct HTTP/GraphQL semantics in practice - graded by reading code and real responses, not by any document existing. DONE only if: a spot-check of representative endpoints shows correct verb usage (GET never mutates state, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE deletes) and correct status codes (201 on create, 204 on empty success, 4xx for client mistakes vs 5xx for server faults, no 200-with-error-in-body); list endpoints are paginated with a server-side maximum page size; filtering and sorting parameters follow one convention across all endpoints; error responses use the unified structure graded in Observability & Errors.
tasks.risk: The website and mobile apps are built to expect the system to respond in a standard, predictable way; where it quietly does something different, users see freezes, wrong data, or error screens that are hard to trace. Each app team then builds its own workarounds, and untangling those later becomes a project of its own, making every future change slower and more expensive.

tasks.description: The API reads as one system: consistent resource naming, casing, pluralization, and verb usage across all endpoints. DONE only if: a full route listing (router dump or generated OpenAPI/GraphQL spec) shows a single casing convention and consistent resource pluralization; no mixed styles such as /getUser alongside /users or verbs embedded in resource paths outside the standard's sanctioned action-endpoint pattern; nesting of sub-resources follows one consistent scheme; any exceptions are documented in the API standard.
tasks.risk: Because the system's building blocks follow no single naming pattern, every developer who connects to it - including new hires and partner teams - must stop and look up each piece individually, slowing delivery on every feature. Renaming things later would break the apps already relying on them, so the inconsistency and its cost become permanent.

tasks.description: Interactive API documentation (Swagger UI, GraphQL playground) is available to FE/QA on non-production environments and generated from code or schema so it cannot go stale. DONE only if: the docs are generated from annotations/decorators/SDL rather than maintained by hand; a spot-check confirms documented endpoints match actual routes and schemas; FE/QA can reach the docs on dev/staging without asking a backend developer. Production exposure of the docs UI and schema introspection is graded in Security & Compliance under 'No exposed management/debug endpoints'.
tasks.risk: Without an always-current, self-service reference explaining how the system works, the people building app screens and the testers must interrupt the core developers with questions for every feature - roughly doubling the time each piece of work takes and making progress depend on a few specific people being available.

tasks.body: Versioning by platform and API type (internal, external)
tasks.description: A documented versioning scheme distinguishes internal APIs from external/mobile-facing ones, so breaking changes can ship without stranding deployed clients. DONE only if: the scheme is written down (which APIs are versioned, version carried in URL or header, what counts as a breaking change); versioned routing is visible in the code, not only in the document; at least one real or planned breaking change demonstrates the mechanism - old and new versions can coexist rather than the old one being edited in place. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Without a way to keep old and new behavior running side by side, any change to how the system talks to the mobile app instantly breaks the app for every user who has not updated it. Users are locked out of the product until an emergency fix is released - and app store approval for that fix can take days.

tasks.description: The backend can tell clients that a newer app version is available and recommended, nudging users forward without blocking them. DONE only if: a server-side mechanism exists (version-check endpoint, response header, or remote config) that returns the recommended minimum version per platform; the thresholds are changeable at runtime through config or an admin path, without redeploying the backend; the response format for the nudge is documented in the API contract so clients actually implement it. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Users linger for months on outdated versions of the app, repeatedly hitting problems that were fixed long ago - so support keeps spending time on already-solved issues, and new features that require the latest app cannot launch because most of the audience never updates.

tasks.description: A server-side kill switch can lock out client versions that are incompatible or dangerously broken, forcing an update. DONE only if: enforcement happens on the backend - requests from versions below the configured minimum are rejected with a distinct, documented status/error code that clients translate into a force-update screen - not merely a client-side check that an old build ignores; the minimum version is configurable per platform at runtime; the rejection path is covered by a test or can be demonstrated against a running environment. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: If a version of the app ships with a serious flaw - one that corrupts data or exposes customer information - there is no way to switch that version off remotely. Affected users keep running the dangerous version for months, and the damage and exposure keep accumulating the whole time.

tasks.description: Request handling is version-aware: the backend knows which client version is calling and validates payloads against that version's contract instead of silently applying the latest rules. DONE only if: the client version/platform is identified on requests (header, route version, or user-agent) and available to handlers; versioned DTOs/schemas or explicit compatibility handling exist where contracts diverged, so old clients are neither broken by newly required fields nor allowed to write payloads the current model cannot represent; incompatible payloads are rejected with the unified error shape rather than partially persisted. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Phones still running an older app keep sending information in the old format; if the system cannot tell which version it is talking to, it may save that information incorrectly or reject perfectly valid requests. The result is corrupted customer records and broken accounts that only surface weeks later, when they are far more expensive to investigate and repair.

tasks.description: Every build is stamped with an identifiable version - build number and/or commit hash - injected automatically and readable at runtime. DONE only if: the CI build config injects the version/commit hash (no manual editing of a version constant); the running service exposes it (info/health endpoint, startup log line, or release tag in the error tracker); the value on a deployed environment verifiably matches the release that is supposed to be there. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: When a problem is reported, nobody can say with certainty which version of the software the affected user or environment was actually running. The team can spend days investigating the wrong version while the real defect stays live and keeps affecting customers.

tasks.description: Old API versions are retired deliberately: a documented policy defines how long a version is supported after its successor ships and how consumers are told. DONE only if: the deprecation policy (support window, communication channel, timeline) is written down; deprecated versions are visibly marked - Deprecation/Sunset headers, docs annotations, or changelog entries; usage of old versions is measurable (logs/metrics by version) so retirement is decided on data; versions past their sunset date are actually gone or carry a documented decision to extend, not silently supported forever. Applies only to versioned mobile/external clients; applicability is declared at kickoff.
tasks.risk: Without a plan for retiring old versions, the team is committed to keeping every version ever released working forever - each one adds testing and maintenance cost to every future release. Meanwhile, partners and users never move to the current version, because nobody ever tells them a deadline exists.

tasks.description: Core technical documentation exists as a named minimum set, not as 'general docs somewhere'. DONE only if: the project space or repo contains, at minimum, (1) a step-by-step guide to running the project locally, (2) an architecture overview, (3) the deployment process, and (4) a description of external dependencies and integrations; each of the four is checked against the current codebase and infrastructure, and a doc that describes an earlier phase of the project counts as missing.
tasks.risk: If the essentials of how to run, update, and connect the system exist only in the current team's heads, every handover, staffing change, or urgent fix starts with days of detective work - the project stays dependent on specific people, and any future takeover costs far more than it should.

tasks.description: The repository README is the entry point: an engineer must be able to go from clone to a running service using it alone. DONE only if: the README (or docs it links directly) states prerequisites, step-by-step setup and run commands, and pointers to the wider documentation; and following it on a clean machine actually yields a running service. A long README that describes the domain but omits working setup steps does not pass.
tasks.risk: Every new person joining the project loses days just getting it to start on their own machine, so team changes and holiday cover become slow and expensive, and work on actual features is delayed each time.

tasks.description: Public and non-obvious code carries doc comments in the stack's standard format (javadoc, jsdoc, docstrings). DONE only if: public modules, services, and non-trivial methods document their purpose and contract; a spot-check shows the comments match current behavior rather than an old implementation; and tricky sections explain why the code does what it does, not merely restate it.
tasks.risk: Developers have to guess how existing parts of the application are meant to be used, and wrong guesses become avoidable defects that reach users and take extra time and money to trace back to their source.

tasks.description: Significant technical choices are recorded as decision records with their context and consequences. DONE only if: an ADR log exists in the repo or project space; it has entries for the major decisions visible in the codebase (framework, datastore, messaging, auth approach, key third parties); each entry states context, decision, and consequences; and decisions made since the previous assessment have entries too.
tasks.risk: When the people who made key technical choices leave, nobody remembers why things are built the way they are - the team wastes time re-debating settled questions or accidentally reverses a decision made for good reason, paying for the same mistake twice.

tasks.description: C4 context and component views show the system's boundaries and how its parts communicate. DONE only if: at least the context and component levels exist; every deployed service and external integration found in the infrastructure/config actually appears on them; and the diagrams match the current system - no removed components still drawn, no added ones missing.
tasks.risk: Nobody has a reliable picture of how the system's parts and external services connect, so decisions about growth or new connections are made on assumptions - and the errors only show up once the system is live and users are affected.

tasks.description: A domain glossary and business-context overview exist for non-technical stakeholders. DONE only if: the glossary defines the project's domain terms and matches the naming actually used in code and API; a context document explains what the system does and for whom in language a non-engineer can read; and both cover the domain concepts present in the current model, not an early draft of it.
tasks.risk: The business side and the developers end up using different words for the same thing, so features get built that match the written request but not what the business actually meant - and the client pays twice: once to build it, once to redo it.

tasks.description: A cookbook fixes the team's agreed coding patterns and folder structure with reference examples. DONE only if: it covers folder layout, the anatomy of a module, and worked examples for recurring tasks (new endpoint, new module, error handling); and a spot-check of the most recently added code shows it actually follows the documented patterns - a cookbook the code ignores does not pass.
tasks.risk: Every developer organizes their work in their own style, so the application becomes steadily harder to navigate and check - each change takes longer than the last, and bringing in new people or extra help gets progressively more expensive.

tasks.description: Non-functional requirements are written down explicitly rather than assumed. DONE only if: NFRs cover at least performance/latency targets, availability, security, and scalability expectations; each is stated measurably (numbers and limits, not adjectives like 'fast'); and they are either agreed with the client or explicitly marked as team-assumed defaults awaiting confirmation.
tasks.risk: The system can do everything on the feature list and still fail the client's unwritten expectations for speed, reliability, or capacity - a gap discovered at launch, when meeting it means expensive rework instead of an early design choice.

tasks.description: This task grades what is in the risk register, not whether a page exists. DONE only if: the register lists the project's currently real technical risks - critical findings known from this or prior assessments that are absent from it fail the task; each risk has an owner, probability/impact, and a mitigation strategy or plan; there is evidence (minutes, decks, tickets) that risks were reviewed and presented to stakeholders since the last assessment; and resolved or obsolete entries are closed rather than left cluttering the list.
tasks.risk: The project's real dangers stay untracked, so when one of them actually happens the team improvises under pressure instead of following a prepared plan - and the client is blindsided by a costly problem nobody warned them about.

tasks.description: Technical debt is tracked and actually worked, not merely declared as a process. DONE only if: debt items exist as actionable tickets (not just TODO comments) with enough context to implement; a prioritization rule exists (e.g., a fixed share of sprint capacity) and recent iterations show debt tickets genuinely closed; and the debt visible in the code during this assessment is reflected in the backlog - significant debt the auditor can see that has no ticket fails the task.
tasks.risk: Known internal problems pile up without ever being scheduled for fixing, so delivery gets slower month by month - until even a simple new feature carries the price tag of a major repair job.

tasks.body: Useful links: credentials, environments, key URLs
tasks.description: One current index page gathers the project's key links: environment URLs, where credentials are stored (vault/secret-manager entries - never the secret values themselves), repositories, CI, monitoring dashboards, and third-party consoles. DONE only if: the page exists in the project space and covers environments, credential locations, monitoring/CI, and key external tools; and a sample of links opened at assessment resolves to live, current destinations - dead or outdated links fail.
tasks.risk: The team loses time daily just finding where systems and access details live, and during an outage nobody can quickly locate the right monitoring screens or stored access - turning minutes of downtime into hours.

tasks.description: Both joining and leaving the project are documented as runnable checklists. DONE only if: the onboarding doc lists the accesses to request, setup steps, and first-task guidance, and is verified against reality (the most recent joiner followed it, or the auditor can trace it end to end); the offboarding checklist enumerates the accesses and credentials to revoke plus knowledge-handover steps; and both reflect the current toolset rather than tools the project no longer uses.
tasks.risk: New team members take weeks instead of days to become productive, and people who leave can quietly keep access to the client's systems and data - an open door that stays open until someone happens to notice.
